brief: Writing so a busy reader cannot misunderstand you

slots.standfirst: Six habits that hold up in front of somebody skimming, half-interested and already deciding whether to keep going.
slots.item1: Why the opening sentence is the only one you actually control
slots.item2: The edit that removes most of the ways to be misread
slots.coverNote: The last one is the reason clear writing is unpopular

slots.body: A reader who has the answer will read the reasoning. A reader who has the reasoning will leave before the answer. Building to a conclusion is how you were taught to write essays and it is the wrong shape for anything somebody has to act on.
slots.k1: Say it in the first line
slots.v1: Not the topic. The finding. The thing you would say if you had one sentence.
slots.v2: The argument reads as support once the claim is already in the reader's head.
slots.v3: Every paragraph written to warm yourself up is one the reader has to skip.

slots.body: Two ideas in a paragraph means the reader has to hold both while deciding which one it was about, and half of them pick wrong. Length is not the problem — a long paragraph about one thing is easier than a short one about two.
slots.v1: If the first sentence does not carry it, the paragraph is doing two jobs.
slots.v2: Wherever you would say 'but' or 'meanwhile', that is a new paragraph.
slots.v3: String them together. If that reads as an argument, the structure works.

slots.body: Somewhat, arguably, fairly, tends to, in many cases. Each one is inserted to be accurate and lands as a lack of conviction. If a claim genuinely needs a limit, state the limit as a fact rather than dissolving it into the sentence.
slots.v1: Then put back only the ones whose absence makes a sentence false.
slots.v2: 'This holds under X' beats 'this may sometimes hold'.
slots.v3: Two hedges in one sentence is a sign you do not believe the sentence.

slots.body: General statements have to be decoded before they can be checked, and most readers do not bother. A concrete example is understood in one pass and remembered afterwards, which is why the specific version is shorter in practice even when it is longer on the page.
slots.v1: Not 'a stakeholder'. The person, the team, the situation you mean.
slots.v2: One is persuasive. Three is a list and reads as padding.
slots.v3: Solution, resource, initiative — words chosen to avoid committing to a meaning.

slots.body: Reading silently, you supply the emphasis the sentence lacks and repair its structure without noticing. Out loud, the repair is impossible: you run out of breath, you stumble on the clause order, and every place you stumble is a place the reader will.
slots.k1: Do it once, all of it
slots.v1: Not the tricky paragraph. The whole thing, start to finish.
slots.v2: Stopping to edit puts you back inside the sentence you are testing.
slots.v3: A sentence you cannot say is a sentence somebody has to read twice.

slots.body: Vague writing cannot be wrong, which is most of why people write it. Every habit here converts a defensible statement into a checkable one, and the cost of being understood is that somebody can now tell you that you are mistaken.
slots.v1: Being understood and being unassailable are not available together.
slots.v2: It protects the writer and costs the reader the point.
slots.v3: There is a real case for cover. Just do not confuse it with good writing.

slots.eyebrow: On the thing sitting in your drafts
slots.body: The one you wrote to get going. It is almost always context the reader already has, and the second paragraph is almost always the real opening.
slots.closingLine: If the piece still makes sense without it, it was never doing anything but warming you up.
slots.signoff: Then read what is left out loud
